Stop Policing AI.
Start Out-Teaching It.

What should a programming assignment require after an LLM has already produced plausible code?

Digital Filters 521337A University of Oulu Spring 2026

01 / The question

Working code is not the same as visible learning.

An LLM can produce Python code for a digital filter in seconds. That does not make the assignment obsolete. It changes what the assignment must ask the student to do.

In Spring 2026, this question became the focus of my Teaching Practice in University Pedagogy. I work mainly with the Python assignments in Digital Filters 521337A, a mathematically demanding engineering course with approximately 120 registered students. The assignments connect equations, code, plots, audio, and signal interpretation.

LLMs can explain sampling, suggest debugging steps, and translate an abstract concept into simpler language. They can also produce fluent explanations and working code that a student cannot evaluate. The pedagogical problem is therefore larger than whether AI is allowed. The real question is what kind of thinking remains visible after AI has been used.

The task should remain educationally meaningful after AI has been used.

02 / From research to design

Three moves from evidence into practice.

1

Make AI visible

Course guidance presented AI as optional support for explanations and debugging. Students remained responsible for understanding and checking the work.

2

Repeat clear rules

Understand why. Fact-check important outputs. Report meaningful assistance transparently. No paid AI tool was required.

3

Reframe the tasks

Selected notebooks asked students to interpret plots, compare results with theory, explain unexpected behaviour, and verify technical plausibility.

Before the course started, I had completed the main work for a scoping review of 195 papers on LLMs in higher education. The literature pointed in two directions. Guided use can support tutoring, feedback, programming, and concept learning. Unguided use can encourage cognitive offloading, over-reliance, weak verification, and confidence without competence.

The assignments were also connected more clearly with real applications such as audio and ECG filtering. Instructions made the intended learning actions more explicit, while keeping AI optional.

03 / What happened

Useful signals, not proof.

Local feedback confirmed that AI-supported study was already part of the teaching context. It also exposed the limits of the available evidence.

20/22 expected to use AI in some form at course entry
14/22 planned to use AI as a personal tutor
16/17 reported frequent AI use in a later broader survey
12/17 agreed that AI can make skipping thinking easier
!
Interpretation limit. The first poll was small. The later survey included only six current or former Digital Filters students. These results guided reflection, but they do not establish a causal improvement in learning.

Questions became less visible

Some students disclosed AI use directly in their assignments, and informal feedback indicated that open permission combined with practical advice was appreciated. Students also asked fewer questions than in previous years. This may indicate clearer materials and more independent work. It may also indicate less visible uncertainty or uncritical acceptance of generated answers. Reduced help-seeking is not automatically evidence of better learning.

“

The most useful result was a limitation.

04 / The reflective lesson

Feedback belongs inside the work.

The surveys did not fail completely. They exposed a weakness in my feedback design.

I had placed too much reflection outside the normal assignment workflow. A voluntary survey competes with deadlines and other priorities. It also reaches only the students who decide to respond.

The next version should place short questions directly inside notebooks, Moodle quizzes, or assignment submissions. Students could report what support they used, what they checked, what they changed, and what remains uncertain. Reflection then becomes part of the learning activity rather than an additional request after it.

This was also the wider lesson from my University Pedagogy studies. Teaching development becomes more credible when research, design, implementation, feedback, and critical reflection form one connected process. It is not enough to add guidance. Learning outcomes, tasks, feedback, and assessment must direct attention to the reasoning that matters.

05 / What comes next

Make verification routine.

The next course iteration should improve AI guidance and design tasks where final code has limited value without explanation.

A

Predict before running. Ask students to state the expected behaviour before executing code.

B

Compare and interpret. Connect observed results with theory, specifications, and engineering judgement.

C

Document checking. Record what support was used, what was verified, and what changed after checking.

D

Study later outcomes carefully. Compare assignment evidence with examination performance while accounting for cohort and course differences.

Three principles colleagues can use tomorrow.

The position is neither a ban nor uncritical acceptance. Assignment design determines whether AI supports thinking or replaces it.

01

Make cheating boring.

Design tasks where an answer without reasoning, verification, and interpretation has little value.

02

Grade the process.

Reward source checking, debugging decisions, validation, and interpretation of results.

03

Embed reflection.

Ask about AI use inside notebooks and submissions, not only through optional surveys.

Rules alone do not create learning. Responsible AI use begins with assignment design.

CA

Constantino Álvarez Casado

Postdoctoral Researcher at the Center for Machine Vision and Signal Analysis, University of Oulu. His work combines signal processing, artificial intelligence, multimodal sensing, research supervision, and university teaching.
